extracted.intended_audience: general readers; mathematicians and journalists interested in the Perelman/Poincaré conjecture controversy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia page summarizing The New Yorker article 'Manifold Destiny', its content, and the ensuing controversies about attribution, editorial process, and professional ethics in the mathematics community. The page recounts events, quotations, reactions, errata, and related correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board consultation / notification procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The page reports that "the thirty-one mathematicians on the editorial board of the Asian Journal of Mathematics received a brief e-mail from Yau and the journal’s co-editor informing them that they had three days to comment on a paper. The e-mail did not include a copy of the paper, reports from referees, or an abstract."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper editorial practice implies providing board members with the paper (or abstract) and referee reports and allowing sufficient time for consideration; notifying without the paper or reports and giving only days to respond is presented as an anti-pattern that invites criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and availability of refereeing reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The article highlights that board members were asked to comment without receiving referee reports and that at least one board member requested to see the paper but was told it was not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial transparency — including making referee reports and the manuscript available to relevant decision-makers — is a substantive standard; withholding these materials undermines trust in the review/publishing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest / editorial impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Joan Birman and others raised concerns that the AJM editorial board apparently assented to publication of a paper by authors known to have "deep personal attachments" to the AJM editors-in-chief, questioning the process and impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and journals should avoid or manage conflicts of interest; apparent personal attachments between authors and editors without clear safeguards provide grounds for critique and reduce confidence in editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate attribution and avoidance of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: The page describes discovery that "a crucial argument of the Cao–Zhu paper was identical to one from a note by Bruce Kleiner and John Lott" and that Cao and Zhu published an erratum acknowledging Kleiner and Lott's priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper scholarly practice requires crediting prior work; failure to attribute identical or substantially similar arguments is treated as a serious lapse, remedied by errata and apologies when confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate claim of originality versus exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Cao and Zhu originally used the abstract phrase "we give a complete proof" and later retracted and revised it to "we give a detailed exposition of a complete proof."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should accurately describe the nature of their contribution; overstating originality (claiming to give a proof when the work is exposition of existing arguments) is an inappropriate claim and subject to public correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of errata, retractions, and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: After similarity with Kleiner and Lott was pointed out, Cao and Zhu published an erratum acknowledging the priority and the AJM editorial board issued an apology; Cao and Zhu later retracted and posted a revised version with a changed abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and authors are expected to correct the record via errata, apologies, retractions, or revised versions when substantive errors or attribution problems are discovered; these are appropriate remediation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ethics and community standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Perelman is quoted expressing disillusionment with "the lax ethical standards of the community," and the article discusses accusations, disputes, and animosities among mathematicians over credit and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mathematical community values integrity, proper attribution, and honest conduct; behavior perceived as unethical (e.g., taking undue credit, tolerating dishonest practices) harms the profession and is a substantive concern reflected in responses and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling disputes over credit and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative centers on who contributed how much to the proof of the Poincaré conjecture and describes public letters, statements, and community debate (e.g., letters from Hamilton, statements posted on Yau's site, notices in AMS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolving priority and credit disputes relies on transparent evidence, community discussion, and published corrections or acknowledgements; public debate and formal statements are part of the resolution process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fairness in journalistic reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Yau's attorneys accused The New Yorker and the authors of "defaming" him, alleging fabricated quotes and molded facts; The New Yorker stood by its story. The article reports NPR's independent translation and analysis and coverage in other outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists reporting on academic controversies should verify quotes and claims, avoid molding facts into narratives known to be inaccurate, and be prepared to substantiate reporting; failures may lead to defamation claims and reputational disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of imagery and editorial depiction in sensitive coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker article included a full-page color illustration of Yau grabbing the Fields Medal hanging around Perelman's neck; the illustration "has garnered controversy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual elements that dramatize or caricature individuals in contentious stories can inflame controversy and should be used carefully to avoid misrepresentation or undue sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community response and post-publication peer commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Following publication, multiple mathematicians issued statements (Stroock, Anderson), Hamilton posted a letter, the AMS meeting panel attempt failed due to refusals to share stage, and Notices of the AMS published letters — demonstrating community scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly and professional communities exercise post-publication review through statements, letters, panels, and notices; this collective scrutiny functions as an important corrective and evaluative mechanism after disputed publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate titling and abstracting of scholarly articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cao–Zhu paper's original title "A Complete Proof of the Poincaré and Geometrization Conjectures — Application of the Hamilton–Perelman Theory of The Ricci Flow" was later retracted and the title revised to a more modest formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles and abstracts should accurately reflect the paper's content and claims; grandiose or misleading titles inviting claims of completing major results without clear justification are subject to critique and revision.
